question: What can one violin do above three players who hardly move?
intro: The C major quartet’s slow movement is in C minor: the first violin spins long ornamental lines over a sombre chordal accompaniment from the other three. It ends on a held G and runs straight into the Menuetto.

sections.label: Opening paragraph · C minor towards G minor
Middle stretch · E♭ major and F minor
Return to C minor and close

cues.title: A slow movement in C minor
cues.text: After the C major Vivace the key turns to C minor. Shulman, quoting Rosemary Hughes, hears the first violin breaking into impassioned arabesques above a dark, brooding melody, “in the manner of a wild Hungarian lament”.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s programme note quotes Hughes on the C minor Adagio (https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf). The report’s global key is C minor (r 0.84) and the first windows read C minor (r 0.88, 0.83); no phrase is timed.

cues.title: Leaning towards G minor
cues.text: Around the half-minute the key estimate leans from C minor towards G minor, the minor dominant. The level swells to a first peak and then dips sharply, so the opening paragraph has an audible shape.
cues.evidence: Local key reads G minor at 0:15–0:40 (r 0.76–0.84) with F♯ in the bass at 0:25, level peaking at −10.4 dB at 0:30 and falling to −30.1 dB at 0:40; boundaries at 0:26 and 0:38. Estimates from audio confirm a key region only.

cues.title: One line above, three below
cues.text: Follow the first violin’s ornamental line, and notice how little the lower three do by comparison: long, linked chords with an occasional answering phrase. The violin’s virtuosity is the movement’s subject.
cues.evidence: Hughes and Shulman describe the violin line rhapsodizing above a “somber chorale” of the other three; the score (IMSLP #05812, pp. 188–189) shows mostly long held notes in the lower three under running violin figuration. The report’s readings in this stretch are steady (C minor, onset density 1.2–4.6 per second).

cues.title: The prominent first violin
cues.text: All twelve Tost quartets, Opp. 54, 55 and 64, give the first violin unusual weight. The scholar Rosemary Hughes, quoted by Shulman, calls this an artistic resource that demands virtuosity and lends “fire and eloquence”; the C minor Adagio is her example.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s note, quoting Hughes, says the first violin has an unusually prominent role in all twelve Tost quartets and singles out the C minor Adagio.

cues.title: The harmony turns to the flat side
cues.text: The strongest change in the movement falls here: the key estimate passes from E♭ major to F minor within about ten seconds, brighter and then darker than the C minor of the opening. The violin keeps its line while the chords move beneath it.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:32 (novelty 1.00), with a quiet window at 1:20 (−26.4 dB) and local keys E♭ major at 1:25–1:30 (r 0.82, 0.71) and F minor at 1:35–1:45 (r 0.80, 0.88, 0.73). These are estimates from audio, not chord labels.

cues.title: Back in C minor, busier
cues.text: From about 1:55 the key estimate settles in C minor again and holds there for about a minute. The violin’s figuration is at its busiest soon after: detected attacks reach more than five per second around 2:15.
cues.evidence: Local key reads C minor from 1:55 to 2:55 (r 0.64–0.90); onset density rises to 5.2 per second at 2:15; boundaries at 1:46 (0.76) and 1:58 (0.38).

cues.title: A held note, then the Menuetto
cues.text: Listen to the last half-minute die away: the marking is morendo, “dying away”, and the movement ends on a fermata. Haydn then writes attacca, so the Menuetto follows without a pause and the two movements are telescoped into one.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #05812, p. 190) shows morendo, a fermata and attacca at the end; Shulman notes that Haydn proceeds without pause to the Menuetto. The report reads G minor/G major at 3:00–3:05 and level −31.8 dB at 3:05; the bar of the fermata is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From C minor to the flat side
transitions.how: After a quiet window the harmony leaves the C minor and G minor of the opening for E♭ major, the relative major, and then darkens to F minor, the subdominant minor. The violin continues its decorated line across the change, so the join is carried by the harmonic colour of the accompaniment rather than by a new theme. The listener hears a change of colour first and a change of key second.
transitions.evidence: The strongest boundary is 1:32 (1.00), after a quiet window at 1:20 (−26.4 dB); local keys read E♭ major at 1:25–1:30 and F minor at 1:35–1:45. The keys are audio estimates and bars are not aligned; the continuity of the violin line is read from the score at passage level.

transitions.title: Home key returns, violin busier
transitions.to: Return to C minor and close
transitions.how: The key estimate passes from F minor through F major back to C minor, and holds there for most of the remaining stretch, before the closing held G. The first violin’s figuration becomes denser as the home key returns, so the return is marked by faster notes rather than by a pause. The close that follows ends on a held G with attacca into the C major Menuetto.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 1:46 (0.76) and 1:58 (0.38); local keys read F minor at 1:40–1:45, F major at 1:50 and C minor from 1:55; onset density rises to 5.2 per second at 2:15. The ending is described from the score’s fermata and attacca; bars are not aligned.

timeline.note: First violin decorates the line while the other three play long, linked chords.
The harmony moves to E♭ and F minor beneath the violin’s continuing figuration.
Morendo: all four fade towards a held G and attacca.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
